title: Pipes, grep & Log Inspection
objectives: Chain commands with pipes, keeping stdout, stderr and exit codes straight
Filter text with grep -r/-i/-v and count, sort and deduplicate with wc/sort/uniq
Follow a live log with tail -f and grep it safely
Work through an error log end-to-end: find, count, group, locate code
body:
Every Unix tool reads stdin and writes stdout, so small tools compose into pipelines that outperform any single giant program. Log triage is the daily proof: an incident hands you 2 GB of text and a question. The answer is never 'open it in an editor' — it is a pipeline you build in seconds.

## The problem

An alert says checkout errors spiked. You have app.log. You need: what the errors are, how many of each, when they started, and which request IDs to pull. That is four questions, each answered by one stage of a pipe.

## Pipes: stdout to stdin

`who | wc -l` — wc receives exactly who's output. Everything is a stream; `2>` redirects stderr separately (errors often bypass the pipe: `cmd 2>err.txt`), and `xargs` turns stdin into arguments (`grep -rl TODO . | xargs rm` style flows).

```bash
cat access.log | grep ERROR | wc -l   # works
grep ERROR access.log | wc -l         # better: no useless cat
```

## grep: the workhorse

```bash
grep ERROR app.log            # lines containing ERROR
grep -i error app.log         # case-insensitive
grep -v DEBUG app.log         # inverse: drop DEBUG lines
grep -rn 'customerId' src/    # recursive, with line numbers, in code
grep -c ERROR app.log         # count matching lines
grep -A 3 -B 1 'panic' app.log  # context: 3 after, 1 before
```

-r searches directories (your log might rotate into app.log.1), -n gives locations you can jump to, -i because humans type inconsistently, -v to silence noise. Basic regex is enough: `grep -E 'ERROR|FATAL'` alternation.

## Counting patterns with sort | uniq -c

uniq only collapses adjacent duplicates, so sort first. This trio is the fastest 'what are the top errors' tool in existence:

```bash
grep ERROR app.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 5

# group by a field, e.g. the status code (whitespace-split field 9)
awk '{print $9}' access.log | sort | uniq -c
```

## Following a live log

```bash
tail -f app.log                    # stream new lines as they land
tail -n 200 app.log                # recent history first
tail -f app.log | grep --line-buffered ERROR   # filtered live view
```

-f keeps reading as the file grows (an incident in real time); -F survives log rotation. On systemd hosts, `journalctl -u myapp -f` does the same for service logs. Note --line-buffered: without it grep buffers and you see nothing until the buffer fills — a classic 'why is my pipe empty' trap.

## End-to-end: triaging app.log

```bash
# 1) recency: what happened just before the alert?
tail -n 200 app.log

# 2) volume: how bad is it?
grep -c ERROR app.log

# 3) top offenders: which messages dominate?
grep ERROR app.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

# 4) impact: which requests are affected?
grep ERROR app.log | grep -o 'req_id=[a-z0-9-]*' | sort -u | head

# 5) follow the fix live
tail -f app.log | grep --line-buffered -v 'healthcheck'
```

Every stage is one decision; the pipeline is auditable and reproducible — which is exactly what an incident timeline needs.

## Best practices

- Avoid useless cat; grep accepts filenames directly.
- Build pipelines one stage at a time, checking output between stages.
- Put -c or wc -l before reading thousands of matching lines.
- Quote every pattern ('req_id=.*409') so spaces and metacharacters survive the shell.
- Use --line-buffered when grep feeds a live tail -f.

## Common mistakes

- uniq without sort — duplicates must be adjacent to collapse.
- Forgetting that stderr bypasses pipes: errors scroll by while you filter stdout.
- Unquoted patterns with spaces or |, which the shell interprets instead of grep.
- grep on a 10 GB file without -m limit or time bound when you only need a sample.

examples.name: log-triage.sh
examples.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

LOG=app.log

# 1) How many ERROR lines in total?
grep -c 'ERROR' "$LOG"

# 2) Top 5 recurring error messages (adjacency: sort before uniq)
grep 'ERROR' "$LOG" \
  | sort \
  | uniq -c \
  | sort -rn \
  | head -n 5

# 3) Everything EXCEPT noisy DEBUG lines
 grep -v 'DEBUG' "$LOG" | tail -n 50

# 4) Case-insensitive sweep across a whole directory, with line numbers
grep -rni 'timeout' /var/log/myapp/ | head

# 5) Follow a live log, filtered in real time
tail -f "$LOG" | grep --line-buffered 'ERROR'

# 6) Which request IDs hit errors? (unique, first 10)
grep 'ERROR' "$LOG" \
  | grep -o 'req_id=[a-z0-9-]*' \
  | sort -u \
  | head -n 10

# 7) stderr vs stdout: keep the output, throw the noise away
ls /tmp/missing 2>/dev/null || echo 'not there (stderr suppressed)'

questions.prompt: Why does `sort file | uniq -c` give correct counts while `uniq -c file` alone does not?
options: uniq only collapses adjacent duplicates, so equal lines must first become neighbors
uniq -c cannot read files, only pipes
sort deletes the duplicates uniq would count
questions.explanation: uniq compares each line only with the previous one. Unsorted input scatters duplicates across the file, so they are never adjacent and survive as separate groups.

questions.prompt: Which grep invocation finds 'timeout' in any case across all files under /var/log/app, showing file names and line numbers?
questions.explanation: -r recurses into directories, -n prints line numbers, -i makes the match case-insensitive.
